rows.searchedFor: can I do some paid freelance work outside my job here?
rows.answer:
Yes, within limits. PostHog is ok with you earning money on the side, but not with it being your main focus.[1] A few hours a month on a paid side gig is acceptable, and side gigs should by default be something you work on in your personal time and should not impact your work at PostHog.[2]

Other points from the handbook:
- Check in with the relevant Exec team member for your team (i.e. James, Tim, or Charles) to get their confirmation before going ahead with any side gig.[3]
- PostHog currently doesn't offer part time work as an option.[1]
- PostHog won't claim ownership of IP you create in your personal time, but you must not introduce any of PostHog's non-open source IP into your work. Anything explicitly MIT-licensed from PostHog is fine to use; anything else is not.[4]
- Anything that comes out of your work at PostHog, such as hackathons, offsites, team projects or internal experiments, is treated as PostHog work by default.[5] To develop such an idea as an external side project, get explicit sign-off first.[6]
- If you want a side gig to become your full-time work one day, let PostHog know so they can create a plan.[7]

rows.searchedFor: a big prospect wants a feature promised by Q3 written into their contract - is that ok?
rows.answer:
No. The handbook says PostHog doesn't contract deliverables, and especially doesn't contract to provide deliverables by a certain date, because on principle a single customer would be forcing the company to build something.[1] Another passage gives the reason as a single customer could otherwise have too much of an impact on team morale and priorities.[2]

Some related points:
- If PostHog has to walk away from a deal because it would have to compromise on these principles, it will.[3]
- PostHog will build things for a big customer as long as it is confident they won't be the only user of that thing, and re-shuffling the roadmap a bit could make sense.[4]
- Customers need to try PostHog before they expect changes.[5]

rows.searchedFor: how does a YC founder get a desk at Hogpatch?
rows.answer:
A YC founder can't apply for Hogpatch. It is invite-only and isn't open to the whole batch; when space opens up, PostHog handpicks a few YC companies to join.[1] There is a waitlist, but you can't apply, since founders are handpicked when there's room.[2]

Once invited:
- The office manager, Judy, sends you and your cofounders a digital wallet pass, which gives 24/7 self-service access.[3]
- There's no booking system for desks and phone booths; you just grab a spot when you arrive.[4]
- Each invite lasts 3 months.[5]

rows.searchedFor: why did US customers lose their older Logs data in February?
rows.answer:
The loss came from a bug in ClickHouse's zero-copy replication, which was triggered by a routine mutation. A routine mutation was run at 10:54 on Feb 19 to materialize an index, and when it finished it triggered a bug in ClickHouse's zero-copy replication. That caused one of the replicas to erroneously believe all of the data parts in the database were no longer referenced.[1]

- From 11:02 to 19:40, the replicas deleted all of the data stored in S3 for the entire database.[2]
- The deletion happened silently in the background without application-level errors, and the team lacked monitoring for the integrity of "cold" data in S3.[3] Data only moves to S3 after 24 hours, and most queries are for recent data, so the volume of query errors was low and no automated alarms fired.[2]
- The problem surfaced when a node crashed and restarted at 19:40 and couldn't start up because of the missing data.[4]
- Contributing factors: experimental configurations (Zero Copy Replication) intended for MVP/Alpha stages were allowed to persist into production.[5] Relying solely on database replication for durability created a single point of failure, and S3 Versioning wasn't enabled, which would have allowed the deleted files to be "undeleted".[6]

The result was loss of Logs data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region.[7] Kafka's 3 days of retention saved recent activity from total loss.[8]

rows.searchedFor: Did PostHog recover any of the US customers' older Logs data that was lost in February?
rows.answer:
The handbook doesn't show that the older data was recovered. It only describes a recovery of the most recent 3 days from Kafka.

- The incident caused the loss of data collected more than 3 days ago in the US region.[1]
- By 21:45 on Feb 19, it was determined that the data was most likely unrecoverable, and disaster recovery procedures started.[2]
- The team decided to cut over to a new table and restore data from Kafka, which had 3 days of retention.[3] The backfill from Kafka history began Feb 20 at 10:05 and completed at 12:21.[4]
- The Kafka 3-day retention saved them from total data loss for recent activity.[5]

rows.searchedFor: we're launching a beta soon - when do we need to start tracking which users are interested in our product?
rows.answer:
You should start tracking product intents as soon as your product is in any sort of public beta. As soon as your product is in any sort of public beta you should start tracking product intents.[1] The reason isn't to hyper-focus on activation numbers at this stage, but to start collecting data for when you later want to determine a good activation metric.[1] Collecting product intents should be a precursor to any sort of public release.[2]

If you want to track interest for a new product on the website, you'll need to add a new entry to PRODUCT_SLUGS in src/lib/productInterest.ts[3].

rows.searchedFor: which of my accounts are big enough to be worth visiting in person?
rows.answer:
The handbook gives two thresholds, so which accounts qualify depends on the context:

- In-person visits work best for accounts paying or likely to pay $50k+/year where you've identified specific expansion opportunities, are navigating renewal conversations, or need to overcome significant technical or organizational hurdles.[1]
- Generally, you should be trying to regularly see customers in your book of business who are $100k+ annually, or could get there.[2]
- You should match the cadence of in-person meetings to the size of the contract: more regular for Very Large, less regular for Large.[3]

Visits are a high-effort, high-reward play, so use them strategically.[1] Your intuition and experience should ultimately guide who you meet in person.[4]

rows.searchedFor: how do I pull the posthog org IDs for all my accounts out of salesforce?
rows.answer:
Run a SQL query against PostHog's data warehouse, which holds the Salesforce data, and export the results as a CSV. The handbook says to query PostHog's data warehouse to pull Salesforce data and create a CSV of all PostHog organization IDs for accounts you own.[1]

The handbook gives this query: SELECT DISTINCT posthog_org_id_c, NULL as empty_column FROM salesforce.account WHERE owner_id = 'your_salesforce_id'[2]

- To find your Salesforce ID, go to your profile and copy the text in the website URL after "/User/".[2]
- Export the results via CSV.[2]
- The empty column is there so the org IDs are comma-delimited, which lets you copy and paste all of them directly into a filter input text field.[2]

rows.searchedFor: how can I see what posthog is doing on a customer's live site?
rows.answer:
You can use PostHog's debug mode on the customer's site. Append ?__posthog_debug=true to a site that has PostHog running, e.g. https://app.mywebsite.com/login?__posthog_debug=true, which can show lots of useful information like logs and config.[1]

If you want to check the configuration specifically, there are two routes:

- Add ?__posthog_debug=true to a URL where PostHog is being called, pull up the console logs, type posthog.config and look for the api_host property.[2]
- If the customer uses session replay, go to the appropriate replay video, select Activity > Inspector > Doctor, search for "config", and look for PostHog Config.[3] In session replay, you can enable doctor and look for the posthog config event.[4]

The api_host value tells you whether they use a reverse proxy: if it shows us.i.posthog or eu.i.posthog, they are not using one.[5] If neither method is available because the customer isn't using session replay and the hosted site isn't publicly accessible, you can ask the customer on the discovery call.[6]

rows.searchedFor: How can I check if a customer has set up a reverse proxy when seeing what PostHog is doing on their live site?
rows.answer:
Open their site in debug mode and check the api_host in the PostHog config.

- Add ?__posthog_debug=true to a URL where PostHog is being called, pull up the console logs, type posthog.config, and look for the api_host property.[1]
- Debug mode can show lots of useful information like logs and config.[2]

To interpret the result, if api_host shows us.i.posthog or eu.i.posthog, they are not using a reverse proxy.[3] If it shows one of their own domains instead of one of PostHog's, that indicates a proxy.[4]

If the customer uses session replay, there's another way: in the replay video, select Activity > Inspector > Doctor, search for "config", find PostHog Config, and expand the api_host.[4]

If neither method is available because the customer isn't using session replay and the hosted site isn't publicly accessible, you can ask the customer on the discovery call.[5]
